import subprocess
import threading

def run_install(argv):
    subprocess.run(argv)

def run_query(argv):
    subprocess.run(argv)

target = run_install
t1 = threading.Thread(target=target, args=(["pacman", "-S", "r22-reuse-a"],))
target = run_query
t2 = threading.Thread(target=target, args=(["pacman", "-Q", "r22-reuse-b"],))
t1.start()
t2.start()
rationale: Python 3.14 static semantics: threading.Thread.__init__ evaluates its arguments at the construction call site and stores target/args/kwargs by reference on the instance (Lib/threading.py:925-928); Thread.run invokes self._target(*self._args, **self._kwargs) (1023-1024); start() runs run() in the new thread (1082). The two constructions are distinct calls: at the t1 statement the local name target resolves to run_install, at the t2 statement it resolves to run_query; rebinding target between the constructions cannot alter either already-built instance. Therefore t1.start() reaches subprocess.run(['pacman', '-S', 'r22-reuse-a']) and t2.start() reaches subprocess.run(['pacman', '-Q', 'r22-reuse-b']); both argv are literal, so truth is exact. The two instances share only the variable name, never a binding: a detector that resolves target at .start() time, or that collapses the two scheduled bindings into one shared or module-global entry, would emit two identical r22-reuse-b package_query rows with the host_mutation row missing and must stay red. Uses only declared supported forms: module top-level defs as targets, literal argv tuples, stored Thread instances started via .start() (r21 FinalBindingReview: scheduled-binding .start maps to thread_start, Thread args/kwargs are evaluated at construction which is the correct timing, and a thread target handed on as a value is skipped by the refs sweep). The two rows are asserted as a set; they are listed in start order only.
